hyperedges.label: One convert run, end to end
The five rules everything obeys (plus the applyEdits rule)
The three-tier conversion model and its gate

nodes.label: Whole-tree passes
nodes.rationale: Cross-file awaits and the project shell are impossible to see one file at a time, so they run after everything is emitted; the shell is last because what it declares depends on what the run produced.

nodes.label: Tier 1 — deterministic AST transform
nodes.rationale: XSJS is ES5 plus the $ global so acorn parses it cleanly; typed transforms cover imports, DB collapse, request/response, direct substitutions, SQL fixes and async propagation — the last derived over the call graph, not guessed, which is exactly what the hand migration got wrong.

nodes.label: The no-AI ceiling (~88% of in-scope files)
nodes.norm_label: the no-ai ceiling (~88% of in-scope files)
nodes.rationale: The deterministic band is not a fallback — it is the bulk of the work, and it is the part that is tedious and error-prone by hand.

nodes.label: The re-parse gate
nodes.rationale: Output is re-parsed as an ES module and the result refused if it does not load; node --check is not equivalent because it treats a file as a script, where XSJS-isms still pass.

nodes.label: Rule 6 — all passes contribute edits to one applyEdits call
nodes.norm_label: rule 6 — all passes contribute edits to one applyedits call
nodes.rationale: Two transforms claiming the same bytes becomes an error instead of one quietly winning.

nodes.label: Missing cross-file awaits (defect class)
nodes.rationale: A Promise used as a value fails silently rather than throwing; 1,275 instances made it the largest defect class in the output by twenty to one, and it is invisible to any per-file view.

nodes.label: Write phase and the two write guards
nodes.norm_label: write phase and the two write guards

nodes.label: The corpus as a retrieval few-shot bank
nodes.norm_label: the corpus as a retrieval few-shot bank
nodes.rationale: 209 matched NEO→CF pairs give real before/after examples; a small model with one on-domain example beats a large model with none. The pairs are also the actual eval — HumanEval and SWE-bench measure agentic multi-file coding and do not transfer.

nodes.label: AI backends — one interface, three implementations
nodes.norm_label: ai backends — one interface, three implementations
nodes.rationale: none / claude / openai. --allowed-tools "" matters: a pure text transform with no filesystem access cannot touch the reference codebases.

nodes.label: The scorecard
nodes.rationale: Structural comparison, not textual; it is how 'most possible success rate in both modes' stops being a feeling.

nodes.label: What to copy from the toolkit
nodes.norm_label: what to copy from the toolkit
nodes.rationale: The parsers are the expensive part and are already validated 587/587; copy and adapt rather than re-derive. Do not take discoverSections(dropPath) — this tool roots at NEO.

nodes.label: dbscan command
nodes.rationale: Exists because the JS tier is where migrations are won or lost, so it tells you how much converts before you start; --show converts one file to stdout.

nodes.label: inventory command
nodes.rationale: Survey that converts nothing; the warnings at the top matter most because an uninferable schema or <APP> segment must be passed rather than guessed.

nodes.label: score command
nodes.rationale: NONE is the only column that is unambiguously ours — a NEO file we produced nothing for; DROP is the hand migration's decision and is not scored.

nodes.label: migration-cleanup-toolkit (ported source)
nodes.rationale: Several modules are ported from it, validated against a 587-view corpus; marked in their header and must not be retuned without re-running score.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting table
nodes.rationale: Notable case: DUPLICATE_FUNCTION is a NEO defect the conversion exposes — a file declaring one function twice, which an XSJS script allows and an ES module rejects.

nodes.label: neo-to-cf-migrator (tool)
nodes.rationale: Converts a SAP NEO (XSJS/XSC) codebase into a SAP CF (CAP/Node.js) codebase mirroring the NEO folder structure. Deterministic first; AI only where a parser genuinely cannot decide.

nodes.label: Rule 4 — the AST locates, the original text is edited by offset
nodes.norm_label: rule 4 — the ast locates, the original text is edited by offset
nodes.rationale: Regenerating JavaScript from the parse tree reformats every file and drops every comment, leaving nothing to diff against the NEO original.

nodes.label: Rule 2 — dry run is the default
nodes.norm_label: rule 2 — dry run is the default
nodes.rationale: A partially converted tree that looks complete is worse than none, so --write is explicit and a blocker stops it unless --force.

nodes.label: Rule 1 — never write to the NEO tree
nodes.norm_label: rule 1 — never write to the neo tree
nodes.rationale: NEO is the input and the only source of truth, so the guard is enforced in core/write.js rather than by convention.

nodes.label: Rule 5 — only bin/ and src/report/ may write to a terminal
nodes.norm_label: rule 5 — only bin/ and src/report/ may write to a terminal
nodes.rationale: Everything else returns data, so adding a UI later is a rendering job rather than a rewrite.

nodes.label: The golden constraints
nodes.rationale: Adopted verbatim from the toolkit: never write to NEO, dry run by default, every change a reviewable patch, NEO is the source of truth, and a rule that cannot decide emits a finding.

nodes.label: CLI now, UI later (the UI boundary)
nodes.norm_label: cli now, ui later (the ui boundary)
nodes.rationale: src/index.js returns data and emits events so a UI later subscribes to the same events and renders the same findings; it costs nothing to keep from day one.

nodes.label: The graphify cache-write incident
nodes.rationale: extract(cache_root=...) wrote a graphify-out/cache/ directory into two reference codebases the KBs forbid modifying — concrete evidence for why the never-write-to-NEO guard lives in code rather than in a convention.

nodes.label: SQL_IDENTIFIER_INTERPOLATED
nodes.rationale: These statements did convert; SQL cannot bind an identifier, so a table or column name is written into the SQL text. Whether that value is reachable is a judgement about the whole application, so the tool names the expression rather than deciding.

nodes.label: What still needs a human
nodes.rationale: Refused statements, AI-CLASSIFIED statements, interpolated identifiers (an injection surface if the value can reach a caller), empty xs-security.json scopes, mta.yaml foreign-schema stubs, and runtime testing — cds build proves the model compiles, it does not run a single SQL statement.

nodes.label: Project shell emission
nodes.rationale: Emitting package.json, mta.yaml, srv/index.cds and xs-security.json is what lets the output be handed to CAP's own compiler, the only thing that knows what CAP will accept.

nodes.label: Phase B — resolve names (the proxies map)
nodes.norm_label: phase b — resolve names (the proxies map)
nodes.rationale: The proxies map is keyed by the NEO id (namespace::filename) because that is the id an .xsodata refers to — which for 92 views in the corpus is not the scenario id inside the XML.

nodes.label: Phase C — emit file text
nodes.rationale: .xsodata files in the same folder are merged into one service.cds because two services in one folder would otherwise fight over the same file name; CAP service names are global, so colliding names are qualified by the first differing folder segment.

nodes.label: The entity-name flattening rule
nodes.rationale: Every . and :: becomes _ and the whole string is uppercased — but the corpus shows the same view flattened two different ways in two modules, so it is not fully deterministic in the reference. The tool makes its own scheme authoritative and self-consistent.

nodes.label: RENAMED IDENTIFIERS table
nodes.rationale: A NEO name starting with a digit is not a legal CDS identifier, so it is renamed — and any UI calling that entity by name has to be told, which is why the table is printed.

nodes.label: The 7c-vs-14 request boundary
nodes.rationale: The two checklist items look contradictory but apply to different layers: entry functions take req directly, everything they fan out to takes primitives. The test is distance from the request, not the function's folder.

nodes.label: The numeric-leading identifier rule
nodes.rationale: CDS/HDI reject identifiers starting with a digit, and the hand migration renamed the same NEO alias to different CF names in different modules. The tool uses a deterministic scheme and emits the before/after table — determinism is for the tool, the table is for the humans whose UI calls those names.

nodes.label: AI-CLASSIFIED marker
nodes.rationale: Anything a model decided is marked in the emitted file, not only in the report — the report is not there when someone reads the code later.

nodes.label: checks/awaits.js — every cross-file async call awaited
nodes.norm_label: checks/awaits.js — every cross-file async call awaited

nodes.label: checks/ceiling.js — what each refusal is worth
nodes.norm_label: checks/ceiling.js — what each refusal is worth
nodes.rationale: Prints the chains where a given refusal code is the only blocker, so effort goes where a fix actually unblocks statements.

nodes.label: checks/leaks.js — the remaining $. surface
nodes.rationale: Asks not only what is left of the $. surface but whether every remaining site sits in a file that carries a finding — a leak with a finding is honest, a leak without one is a lie.

nodes.label: Finding levels — note / warning / blocked
nodes.rationale: Findings are as much the deliverable as the code; a finding's `fix` field tells the developer what to change in NEO so the next run converts it, which is the difference between a report and a to-do list.

nodes.label: JDBC chain object (SQL, binds, columns, reads, gaps)
nodes.norm_label: jdbc chain object (sql, binds, columns, reads, gaps)
nodes.rationale: resolved is simply 'no gap that is not a note'; deliberate refusals each carry their own code — run-time SQL, computed bind index, a read where the row no longer exists, a computed getX index, a ResultSet method CAP does not have.

nodes.label: The verify sweep (ten steps, non-zero exit)
nodes.norm_label: the verify sweep (ten steps, non-zero exit)

nodes.label: The FACTS block
nodes.rationale: The model's biggest failure mode is inventing names, so the prompt asserts as fact everything already known — resolved imports, real table names, procedure signatures and OUT-vs-result-set, the function's call sites. Anything not in FACTS must be flagged rather than invented.

nodes.label: Task registry (task-specific prompts, not one convert prompt)
nodes.norm_label: task registry (task-specific prompts, not one convert prompt)
nodes.rationale: One generic instruction is what large models tolerate and small models fail; each task gets its own tight prompt, output shape and validator (sql-fold, column-resolve, chain-collapse, req-boundary, body-convert). Most return a fragment or JSON, not code, which is what makes a 7B model viable.

nodes.label: The three-tier model
nodes.rationale: AI is not the only option, and treating it as the only option is the failure mode; AI does the smallest job only AI can do.

nodes.label: Tier 2 — AI fills holes
nodes.rationale: Two things changed in the building, both in the same direction: the model returns one word per interpolated SQL value rather than code, and the answer re-enters the analysis rather than the file, so it must pass the same bar as a statement no model ever saw.

nodes.label: Tier 3 — human
nodes.rationale: Anything Tier 2 returns that fails validation twice.

nodes.label: The 24/25-item migration checklist
nodes.rationale: No checklist item was left correct in the assistant's raw output — every one required a manual edit or verification. The assistant's value is bulk file generation, not correctness of these details.

nodes.label: cleanup-kb (clean up the assistant's output)
nodes.rationale: Rejected as the tool's workflow because it depends on a GUI wizard in BAS that cannot be scripted into folder-in/folder-out; its 25-item checklist is still reused as the validation pass, and its intake model was never validated against real assistant output.

nodes.label: Corpus B (ICBC) — NEO input shape only
nodes.norm_label: corpus b (icbc) — neo input shape only
nodes.rationale: Migrated with SAP's assistant plus Claude Code cleanup, so its CF side shows what the assistant emits, not what this tool should emit — which also resolves the 584 .hdbview that exist in CF and nowhere in NEO.

nodes.label: migration-kb (from-scratch knowledge base)
nodes.rationale: Replaces SAP's HANA Application Migration Assistant rather than assisting it, on the grounds that its bulk mechanical conversion is exactly the unreliable part.

nodes.label: Out-of-scope artifact types
nodes.rationale: 116 files inventoried but not converted, so nothing vanishes silently; scoping them out loudly is better than a half-answer.

nodes.label: Scope decisions (§0)
nodes.rationale: Independent conversion rather than cleanup of SAP's assistant output; two first-class modes; Corpus A is the output-shape reference and Corpus B only a NEO-input data point; .xsjob/.xshttpdest/privileges/.xsaccess and .hdbtable are out entirely.

nodes.label: AI mode (--ai)
nodes.rationale: Deterministic mode is not a degraded mode — it converts ~96% of JDBC statements on both reference corpora with no model at all.

nodes.label: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW marker
nodes.rationale: A refusal is left as the original NEO code with reasons directly above it, ending in what to change in NEO so the next run converts it — on a large tree that is often faster than converting by hand.

nodes.label: npm run verify (the whole sweep)
nodes.rationale: cds build was a manual step and manual steps rot; folding it into one command that exits non-zero makes the only real oracle part of every change.

nodes.label: Rules for adding an AI task
nodes.norm_label: rules for adding an ai task
nodes.rationale: Ask for an answer never for code; never ask what Tier 1 can decide; validate something semantic (the SQL grammar overrules the model — a hole after FROM cannot be a bind parameter, a hole after = cannot be an identifier); 'unknown' is a real answer, distinct from never having asked.

nodes.label: cds build --production — the only real oracle
nodes.norm_label: cds build --production — the only real oracle
nodes.rationale: CAP's own compiler is the only thing that knows what CAP accepts; the first run found five defects nothing else could see, including a CDS type that does not exist.

nodes.label: The ceiling rule
nodes.rationale: Never ask a model about what Tier 1 can decide, and never about a statement with a second blocker — the answer would convert nothing. Measure with checks/ceiling.js before building anything for a bucket of refusals; four times it replaced planned work with something smaller and deterministic.

nodes.label: Measure before building
nodes.rationale: Also: read the output of the statements a change just unblocked — a refusal hides everything downstream of it, and three real bugs were found exactly that way.

nodes.label: Rule 3 — a rule that cannot decide emits a finding, not a guess
nodes.norm_label: rule 3 — a rule that cannot decide emits a finding, not a guess
nodes.rationale: The whole tool's credibility rests on it: a refusal costs a developer ten minutes; a wrong conversion costs a day and may never be found.

nodes.label: Tier 2 has no emitter
nodes.rationale: Tier 1 is byte-identical in both modes, enforced by construction: a model's answer re-enters as an input to Tier 1, which decides; if the statement still does not resolve the answer is discarded and the worst a wrong answer can do is waste a call.

nodes.label: The deterministic gate
nodes.rationale: A model's answer is a proposal; it must pass a deterministic gate. The model is a suggestion engine inside a deterministic pipeline, never writes a file directly, and its output faces the same checks as Tier 1's.

nodes.label: The unit is the function, not the file
nodes.norm_label: the unit is the function, not the file
nodes.rationale: Files reach 25-49 KB so one prompt has no verification granularity and blows a local model's context; file-level also discards everything Tier 1 already proved. A function is coherent, verifiable (name, arity, return shape), small, recoverable in one retry, and parallelisable.

nodes.label: Laundering a mechanical transform into a probabilistic one
nodes.norm_label: laundering a mechanical transform into a probabilistic one
nodes.rationale: Handing the model every unresolved finding spends tokens on work a parser already does deterministically and converts a mechanical transform into a probabilistic one — the tempting failure mode.

nodes.label: Designing for a small local model
nodes.norm_label: designing for a small local model
nodes.rationale: Target the small-model case rather than treat it as a downgrade: the remaining tasks are local pattern transformation with the facts supplied. Small models are worse at declining, so 'flag rather than guess' must be enforced by the pipeline, not requested in the prompt — never accept output merely because it parses.

nodes.label: The objective function is developer hours saved
nodes.norm_label: the objective function is developer hours saved
nodes.rationale: Every API is hand-tested afterwards regardless, which inverts the usual trade-off: converting 70% mechanically and flagging the other 30% loudly beats converting 95% and hiding where it guessed, because a wrong-but-confident output costs more to find than an honest gap.

nodes.label: Never invent a rule not demonstrated by a real file
nodes.norm_label: never invent a rule not demonstrated by a real file
nodes.rationale: Both the NEO source and the CF result are present, so always diff them directly; never infer the NEO source from the migrated output. Paired with: if fixing something requires understanding what the business logic is doing, that is a red flag — flag it, don't guess.

nodes.label: Tables do not come from NEO
nodes.norm_label: tables do not come from neo
nodes.rationale: Corpus A has 6 .hdbtable in NEO and 58 in CF; Corpus B has zero and 721. Table DDL is produced by a separate tool from the live HANA catalog, so the tool should detect the gap and say so rather than generate them.

nodes.label: Blockers vs warnings
nodes.rationale: A blocker means the output is not safe to hand over — an entity projecting a view that does not exist, a service.js that does not parse. --force writes anyway; use it knowingly.

nodes.label: Hole (a marked unresolved node)
nodes.rationale: Everything Tier 1 cannot decide becomes a hole carrying the NEO excerpt, the reason, and the surrounding converted context.

nodes.label: JDBC chain collapse to await cds.run
nodes.norm_label: jdbc chain collapse to await cds.run
nodes.rationale: Recognised by data flow, not text: getConnection → prepareStatement → setX → executeQuery → next loop → getX, with array-vs-object decided from the statement kind rather than from memory.

nodes.label: Statically foldable concatenation (sql-fold)
nodes.rationale: Most of the 109 concatenation sites have every operand as a literal or an expression node, so folding into a template with ? binds is an AST transform, not a reasoning task — Tier 2's real residue is tens of sites, not hundreds.

nodes.label: Analysis / emission split (db.js vs emitdb.js)
nodes.rationale: Three consumers read the same chain object — the emitter, the report and the AI tier — so analysis and emission live in separate files; the emitter never re-derives a column name or a bind order.

nodes.label: Positional column access (897 getX(N), zero by name)
nodes.norm_label: positional column access (897 getx(n), zero by name)
nodes.rationale: Resolving getInteger(3) requires parsing the SELECT list; a parser does it identically every time, a model has to infer it, and when it is wrong the code still runs and returns the wrong column. This is the strongest argument for a deterministic transform and against handing files to a model.

nodes.label: transform/db.js as the centrepiece
nodes.rationale: 505 sites, the highest-risk and highest-value module; it gets its own test file with real corpus fixtures and is worth writing before anything else in the JS tier.

nodes.label: Phase A — parse every file into data
nodes.norm_label: phase a — parse every file into data

nodes.label: The calc-view 1:1:1:1 pipeline
nodes.rationale: 454 .calculationview → 454 .hdbcalculationview + 454 TABLE_FUNCTION_*.hdbfunction + 454 db/cds proxies. Not approximately — exactly. ~53% of all NEO files in Corpus A and the single biggest, safest win available.

nodes.label: Backwards information flow (xsodata keys into the CDS proxy)
nodes.norm_label: backwards information flow (xsodata keys into the cds proxy)
nodes.rationale: A CDS proxy's key columns are declared in the .xsodata that projects the view, not in the view itself; emitting while walking would mean either a missing key or a forward reference — which is why parse and emit are separate phases at all.

nodes.label: Intake phase
nodes.rationale: Units are classified by the extensions inside a folder, never its name, because the corpus has Views/View as distinct folders and .xsodata living in a dozen differently-named folders.

nodes.label: The verified NEO → CF folder mapping
nodes.norm_label: the verified neo → cf folder mapping
nodes.rationale: db/cds drops the <APP> wrapper, srv/lib/<SCHEMA>/<APP> keeps it, and the CF bucket name equals the real NEO top-level folder name — never relabelled into Env_Config/Inbound/Outbound.

nodes.label: The output tree layout
nodes.rationale: srv/index.cds exists because CAP does not walk srv/lib on its own.

nodes.label: Path asymmetry — db/ drops <APP>, srv/lib keeps it
nodes.norm_label: path asymmetry — db/ drops <app>, srv/lib keeps it
nodes.rationale: Both directions verified against a shipped CF tree and both easy to get wrong; a wrong <APP> silently merges unrelated subtrees, which is why intake refuses to guess it.

nodes.label: .xsjs placement — settled by evidence
nodes.rationale: All 35 surviving .xsjs landed as their own handler file mirroring the NEO path rather than folding into the service layer. The 25 that did not survive were a dropped module and scratch files — excluding a module is the user's call via config, never the tool guessing.

nodes.label: The complete artifact taxonomy
nodes.rationale: Counted from disk, not from documentation. Only three types carry JavaScript, so the 'AI problem' is ~12% of in-scope files — scoping it correctly stops AI leaking into the other 88%.

nodes.label: Checklist item 16 — result object vs array
nodes.norm_label: checklist item 16 — result object vs array
nodes.rationale: A SELECT yields an array; a CALL with OUT params yields an object. The tool knows because it is converting the .hdbprocedure files in the same run, so the signature is a fact in hand. The shipped hand migration got this wrong twice in one file.

nodes.label: The eight-phase build order
nodes.rationale: Phase 2 is the first release producing real output, phase 6 the first honest no-AI number, phase 7 the first honest answer to 'is the model worth it'.

nodes.label: The nine-pass pipeline
nodes.rationale: Dependency order is procedures → functions → views → services, parents first, because the procedure signatures gathered in pass 2 are what settle checklist item 16 in pass 4 deterministically.

nodes.label: Corpus A (TECK) — the output-shape reference
nodes.rationale: 848 NEO files hand-migrated; the only reference for what this tool's output should look like.

nodes.label: The graphify survey of the CF tree
nodes.norm_label: the graphify survey of the cf tree
nodes.rationale: Blind to NEO — it recognised 5 of 848 files and would need an extension shim. On the CF side it produced 489 nodes and 1542 edges from 91 files and surfaced a validation layer neither knowledge base documents.

nodes.label: Bugs in the hand-migrated reference
nodes.rationale: Worth naming because the tool must not learn from them: a SELECT result bound as a scalar, result.USERCOUNT without the [0], and a silent behaviour change in the simplest file in the corpus. This is what 'hand the file to a model and ask it to convert' produces.

nodes.label: The three scorecard exclusions
nodes.rationale: Without them the scorer lies: files with no NEO ancestor, NEO_DRIFTED views (the hand-migrated CF is a 2026-08 snapshot, not ground truth), and known reference defects — emitting the correct rows[0].USERCOUNT would otherwise score as a mismatch.

nodes.label: CF-only files with no NEO ancestor
nodes.norm_label: cf-only files with no neo ancestor
nodes.rationale: ValidationUtil, Middleware, rate limiting and the rest were written by hand during the migration, not translated. The tool must not scaffold them; they matter because they are noise when diffing CF against NEO to derive a rule, and because they set the ceiling honestly — a perfect run still does not produce the finished CF app.

nodes.label: JS pass order (imports → request → http → db → async)
nodes.norm_label: js pass order (imports → request → http → db → async)
nodes.rationale: A pass that moves text must run after the passes that rewrite inside what it moves and must replay those rewrites into the copy (ctx.inlineRewrites); get it wrong and the moved copy silently keeps the old $. idiom.

nodes.label: Rewrite around a sub-expression, never over it
nodes.norm_label: rewrite around a sub-expression, never over it
nodes.rationale: A pass replacing a whole statement locks every other pass out of its interior, so request.js emits pairs of edits bracketing the argument it keeps.

nodes.label: The XSJS API surface is a closed set
nodes.norm_label: the xsjs api surface is a closed set
nodes.rationale: The single most important fact in the document: XSJS is not an open-ended language problem but a small, fixed, enumerable API of about 15 idioms, all with a known target form.
